items.title: Ministers bring together leaders to rewire youth crime prevention
items.summary: Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards convened local leaders and experts in Manchester to tackle youth crime Roundtable explored how greater local leadership could help services work together, intervene earlier and prevent offending Kate Gre
items.bodyHtml:
• Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards convened local leaders and experts in Manchester to tackle youth crime
  • Roundtable explored how greater local leadership could help services work together, intervene earlier and prevent offending
  • Kate Green appointed Expert Adviser on Youth Justice Devolution to help shape government reforms in England

Local leaders and experts from across youth justice, policing, children’s services and education were brought together by the Government in Manchester today (Thursday 17 September) to help shape plans to prevent more young people being drawn into crime.

Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards convened the roundtable alongside Children and Families Minister Josh MacAlister and Policing and Crime Minister Sarah Jones, exploring how services can work better together to identify children at risk earlier - and where giving local and regional leaders greater freedom could help prevent offending and protect victims.

As part of the Government’s drive to take this work forward, Kate Green has been appointed Expert Adviser on Youth Justice Devolution in England, providing independent advice to Ministers on how greater local leadership could improve youth justice and crime prevention.

Her appointment forms part of the Government’s wider ambition to rewire the state, shifting power and accountability from Whitehall to local leaders and giving communities greater freedom to shape services around their needs.

Jake Richards, Youth Justice Minister, said:

Too often, vulnerable children encounter a system where different services are working hard but not always working together. If we are serious about cutting crime, we need to identify those at risk earlier and intervene before they become trapped in a cycle of offending.

Today I brought together local leaders and experts who know their communities best to hear what works and what gets in their way. By breaking down barriers and giving local leaders greater freedom to join up services, we can prevent more young people being drawn into crime and ultimately protect more victims.

The Ministers also visited SHiFT in Manchester earlier in the day, where they met practitioners working intensively with children and young people at the highest risk of entering custody or becoming entrenched in crime.

Ministers saw first-hand how multi-disciplinary, joined-up support can help steer vulnerable young people away from offending.

Children and Families Minister Josh MacAlister said:

Every young person deserves to grow up supported by the adults around them, like teachers and social workers who can help stop them from being drawn into crime.

We need better and earlier intervention for vulnerable children - from the children’s social care system to youth justice. That’s what today’s discussion in Manchester was about: giving local leaders the freedom to build that support around children before it’s too late.

Policing Minister Sarah Jones said:

Every young person deserves the chance to thrive, no matter where they grow up. I have seen first-hand the difference youth services can make to young people. They provide opportunities at times when other doors have shut or a trusted voice when in day-to-day life they may not exist. They can genuinely turn lives round steering people away from crime and giving them hope for the future.

Kate Green, Expert Adviser on Youth Justice Devolution for England, said:

Young people deserve the opportunity to fulfil their potential and that means intervening early, addressing the factors that place them at risk and ensuring services work together effectively around their needs.

I am pleased to be taking on the role of Expert Adviser for England and look forward to supporting ministers and officials as they consider the future of youth justice reform. Today’s roundtable demonstrated the appetite for new approaches, and I am keen to help share evidence, learning and practical experience that can improve outcomes for young people across the country.

Notes to Editors

  • SHiFT Manchester is a partnership between national charity SHiFT, Manchester City Council and the Greater Manchester Violence Reduction Unit. It uses an intensive, relationship-based approach to work with children and young people at the highest risk of entering custody or becoming entrenched in crime.

  • The Government’s “rewiring the state” programme aims to shift power, funding and accountability from Whitehall to local leaders, including by expanding the role of strategic authorities.

  • Kate Green has been appointed Expert Adviser on Youth Justice Devolution for an initial 18-month period. She will advise Ministers on how strategic authorities could play a greater role in youth justice and crime prevention, including joining up services, pooling resources, reducing duplication and strengthening accountability.

  • The Adviser will work with officials across the Ministry of Justice, Home Office and Department for Education. The role is unremunerated.

  • This week saw the announcement of the locations of 42 more Young Futures Hubs, providing mentoring, wellbeing support, trusted adults and positive opportunities for young people in communities affected by violence: Thousands more young people to access help with life’s biggest challenges - GOV.UK

  • The Halving Knife Crime Plan brings together action across Government and society to stop people turning to knife crime and to ensure that perpetrators are caught and brought to justice, including a range of measures that will tackle the root causes of knife crime to ensure young people who are vulnerable to being drawn into crime are identified and offered support in a more systematic way.

Key measures include:

  • Supporting early intervention and prevention by continuing the work of Violence Reduction Units and Young Futures Panel Pilots, backed by over £66 million for the Serious Violence Reduction Programme and the Serious Violence Duty this financial year.

  • Multi-agency Young Futures Panels proactively identify children and referring young people at risk of being drawn into crime connecting them with support earlier. By the end of October 2025, 53 pilot Panels were operational across England and Wales. Pilot Panel delivery has continued in 2026/27, with a further 12 Panels now operational.

items.title: Senior Traffic Commissioner launches consultation on local bus service performance standards
items.summary: The consultation seeks views from operators, local authorities, passenger groups and other stakeholders on whether current standards remain fit for purpose and how they should evolve to reflect changes in the industry, legislation and techn
items.bodyHtml:
The consultation seeks views from operators, local authorities, passenger groups and other stakeholders on whether current standards remain fit for purpose and how they should evolve to reflect changes in the industry, legislation and technology.

Statutory Document No. 14, which sets out how traffic commissioners approach regulatory action where services fail to meet expected standards, has not undergone a significant review for over a decade. The review forms part of the Traffic Commissioners’ strategic objective to ensure that statutory guidance remains relevant, proportionate and effective.

Reviewing bus punctuality and reliability standards

The consultation focuses in particular on whether the longstanding expectation that 95% of services operate within a window of one minute early to five minutes late remains appropriate in 2026

It also explores:

  • how standards should apply to different types of services, including frequent and flexible routes
  • what constitutes a ‘reasonable excuse’ for poor performance
  • what positive actions by operators should be recognised as mitigation

In addition, the call for evidence considers whether clearer guidance is needed where performance falls below expectations, including the role of improvement plans before formal regulatory action is taken.

Wider regulatory considerations

The consultation also seeks views on a range of related regulatory matters, including:

  • Compliance with Bus Open Data obligations: how traffic commissioners should respond where operators fail to meet their obligations under the Public Service Vehicles (Open Data) (England) Regulations 2020
  • Traffic management: how powers under the Traffic Management Act 2004 could be used to obtain information from local authorities where network issues affect service performance
  • Franchising arrangements: the appropriate regulatory response where services operate without the required authority in franchised areas

The consultation also examines how emerging technology, such as real-time passenger information, and evolving operating environments should influence regulatory expectations.

Collaboration and future standards

The Senior Traffic Commissioner has already engaged with stakeholders in developing the proposals and is now inviting broader input to help shape future guidance.

The aim is to ensure that the regulatory framework:

  • supports reliable and efficient local bus services
  • reflects modern operating conditions
  • promotes fairness and consistency across the industry

Kevin Rooney, Senior Traffic Commissioner for Great Britain, said

“Local bus services play a vital role in connecting communities and supporting economic activity. It is important that our regulatory approach keeps pace with changes in the industry and continues to promote reliable and high-quality services for passengers.

“This consultation provides an opportunity for all stakeholders to share their views on how performance standards should be applied in the future. I encourage anyone with an interest to contribute.”

How to respond

The consultation is open to responses from individuals and organisations. Stakeholders are invited to submit their views on any of the questions set out in the document.

Responses can be submitted by email or post, with full details provided in the Local bus service performance standards: consultation - GOV.UK.

The evidence gathered will inform updates to statutory guidance and statutory directions issued by the Senior Traffic Commissioner.

items.title: DBS launches campaign to help parents and carers make informed decisions when hiring self-employed workers

items.bodyHtml:
Parents and carers across England, Wales, the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are being encouraged to take an additional safeguarding step when hiring self-employed workers and personal employees, as the Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) launches its new Every Check Helps public awareness campaign.

The campaign aims to help parents and carers understand what information may be available when employing someone such as a tutor, sports coach, music teacher, personal assistant or carer, and how that information can support safer recruitment and safeguarding decisions.

The campaign follows legislative changes introduced in January 2026, which enabled eligible self-employed workers and personal employees to apply for Enhanced DBS checks and, where eligible, Enhanced DBS checks with Children’s and/or Adults’ Barred List checks for the first time.

Research and stakeholder insight identified that many parents and carers are unaware that eligible self-employed workers can obtain an Enhanced DBS check, and some may feel unsure about asking to see one when making recruitment decisions. The campaign aims to increase awareness, understanding and confidence among parents and carers, helping them make safer and more informed choices.

At the heart of the campaign is a simple message: “They can get a DBS check. You can ask to see it.” The campaign encourages parents and carers to consider DBS information as one part of a wider decision-making process when choosing someone to work with their child or vulnerable family member.

Importantly, parents and carers cannot apply for a DBS check on behalf of someone else. Where eligible, self-employed workers and personal employees must apply themselves through a DBS Umbrella Body. Parents and carers can then ask whether an individual has a DBS certificate and whether they are willing to share it.

Alongside the campaign, DBS has published guidance explaining what parents and carers should look for when viewing a DBS certificate, including checking they are seeing the original certificate, confirming it relates to the correct workforce, checking the certificate issue date and understanding how the DBS Update Service may provide additional reassurance.

The guidance is designed to help parents and carers better understand what they can do, what they should look for on a DBS certificate and how DBS information can be considered alongside other recruitment and safeguarding considerations.

Minister for Safeguarding and Violence Against Women and Girls, Satvir Kaur said:

As a mother, I know how important it is to feel confident about the people we trust with our children. 

With self-employed people who work with children now able to get enhanced checks, parents and carers will have options to make the safest choice for their families.

It’s part of this Government’s ongoing work to keep children safe, backed by record funding and stronger laws.

Susie Blamire, Associate Director – Strategic Lead for Safeguarding at DBS said: 

The introduction of Enhanced DBS checks for eligible self-employed workers is an important step forward. It means that tutors, coaches, music teachers, carers and others working independently can now provide additional safeguarding information.

A DBS certificate is only one part of the picture, but it can be a valuable part. It should be considered alongside references, recommendations, qualifications, experience, and personal judgement to help build a fuller understanding of an individual’s suitability.

Every question asked and every piece of information considered can contribute to safer decisions and better protection for children and vulnerable people.

Parents and carers are encouraged to review the guidance on GOV.UK to better understand what DBS information may be available, how it can support informed decision-making and what to look for when someone chooses to share a DBS certificate.

Background

  • From 21 January 2026, eligible self-employed workers and personal employees became able to apply for Enhanced DBS checks and, where eligible, Enhanced DBS checks with Children’s and/or Adults’ Barred List checks.
  • The Every Check Helps campaign aims to help parents and carers make informed decisions when hiring individuals to work with their child or vulnerable family member.
  • Parents and carers cannot apply for a DBS check on someone else’s behalf. Eligible individuals must apply themselves through a DBS Umbrella Body.
  • An Enhanced DBS certificate should be considered alongside references, qualifications, experience, recommendations and personal judgement.
  • Campaign resources include GOV.UK guidance, a parent and carer leaflet, partner communications materials and practical advice on what to check when viewing a DBS certificate.

Chair appointed to lead Tees, Esk and Wear Valleys Trust inquiry
items.summary: His Honour Judge John Potter has been appointed chair of the public inquiry into serious failings in mental health care at Tees, Esk and Wear Valleys NHS Foundation Trust (TEWV). The public inquiry, which will give survivors and families th
items.bodyHtml:
• His Honour Judge John Potter has been appointed chair of the public inquiry into serious failings in mental health care at Tees, Esk and Wear Valleys NHS Foundation Trust (TEWV).
  • The public inquiry, which will give survivors and families the opportunity to be heard and drive urgent improvements, will formally start on 21 September.

His Honour Judge Roderick John Conwy Potter has been appointed to chair the public inquiry into mental health care at Tees, Esk and Wear Valleys NHS Foundation Trust (TEWV).

The inquiry, launched by the government in December 2025, will aim to establish what happened in serious failings in mental health care at TEWV, why failings occurred and what needs to change to help ensure patients receive safe, high-quality care.

A retired Circuit Judge and former Deputy Judge of the Criminal Division of the Court of Appeal, Judge Potter has over forty years’ experience in public service, judicial leadership, and the administration of justice.

With Judge Potter’s appointment, the public inquiry will formally start on 21 September.

The Department of Health and Social Care has been working with patients, survivors, and families to help shape its approach to the public inquiry, including engaging with patients and families on matters they would like the inquiry to consider and the qualities they would want to see in a chair.

Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Yvette Cooper said:

The families who were let down by the Tees, Esk and Wear Valley NHS Foundation Trust have suffered immeasurable pain.

Judge Potter has been asked to deliver a comprehensive report into why and how things went so wrong across the trust’s mental health services, and what changes must be made.

His Honour Judge Potter said:

I am honoured to have been appointed to Chair the Tees, Esk and Wear Valleys Inquiry. I am conscious of the responsibility that comes with this role and of the experiences of the patients, families and others affected by the matters the Inquiry will examine.

My first priority will be to meet and listen to those affected. Their voices and experiences will be central to the Inquiry’s work and will help inform the development of its Terms of Reference.

The Inquiry will approach its task independently, thoroughly and fairly, and with respect for everyone who takes part. I will work with the Inquiry team to put the necessary arrangements in place so that our work can begin as promptly as proper preparation allows.

This follows this government’s progress to improve mental health services, including:

  • 159 new NHS mental health facilities across England, backed by £343 million, to help fewer people reach crisis point.
  • The Suicide Prevention Strategy for England and improving support for those affected by self-harm or bereaved by suicide.
  • NHS mental health spending will rise to a record £16.1 billion in 2026 to 2027, a real terms increase of around £140 million.
  • Later this year, the Mental Health Strategy for England will set out how the government will build a more integrated mental health system that intervenes earlier, cuts waiting times for support, and helps people stay active in education, work, family and community life.

ENDS

items.title: Chiltern Railways brought into public ownership
items.summary: Chiltern Railways will move into public ownership this Sunday with plans for a more reliable service across the network people will benefit from 25 more daily services from December alongside cleaner stations, upgraded trains and better on-
items.bodyHtml:
• Chiltern Railways will move into public ownership this Sunday with plans for a more reliable service across the network
  • people will benefit from 25 more daily services from December alongside cleaner stations, upgraded trains and better on-board wifi
  • latest operator’s services to move into public ownership under this government – following Govia Thameslink Railway services transferring in May – as we deliver improvements now and build Great British Railways for the future

Chiltern Railways services will move into public ownership this Sunday (20 September 2026), as the government drives forward change to bring the essentials in life back under stronger public control and finally deliver the rail services people deserve.

Connecting London Marylebone with communities across Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire, Warwickshire and the West Midlands, Chiltern Railways will become the sixth operator whose services transfer into public ownership, which will support more reliable trains for the thousands of people who rely on them every day to get to work, school and see family and friends.

The transfer will pave the way for a package of improvements for Chiltern passengers, including more services and seats, new trains, upgraded stations and better facilities on board. Public ownership also provides a fresh opportunity to deliver East West Rail and its benefits to passengers.

For many who use Chiltern services, overcrowding has become a daily frustration, especially in peak hours. To tackle this, 25 additional daily services will be introduced from December, providing 10,000 extra seats each weekday. The rollout of new state-of-the-art trains will increase capacity while improving accessibility and providing better wifi on board.

The transfer marks another milestone on the journey to Great British Railways (GBR) and making life’s essentials affordable again. Bringing operators’ services into public ownership ahead of its creation is already delivering benefits for people, with fares frozen for the first time in 30 years, 76,000 extra seats a week introduced across the network and a fleet of new GBR trains set to be built in Britain to serve major cities across the north whilst supporting thousands of jobs.

From this Sunday, passengers whose train is cancelled will also be able to use another operator’s service at no extra cost.

Rail Minister, Lord Hendy, said:

From this Sunday, Chiltern Railways passengers will be travelling on rail services back in public hands.

Every transfer into public ownership gives us the chance to tackle the bread-and-butter issues people care about – more frequent, comfortable trains that turn up on time.

As we set up Great British Railways, we’re putting passengers first. It will not happen overnight, but we will build a railway the country can trust and rely on and that will create growth, jobs and homes.

Following the transfer into public ownership, Chiltern Railways passengers will benefit from:

  • More services and seats: a new timetable from December will provide 25 extra services each weekday including half hourly service throughout the day on the Chiltern Mainline between London and Birmingham. This will provide almost 10,000 extra seats every weekday, nearly 5,000 on Saturdays and more than 3,000 on Sundays, helping to tackle overcrowding.
  • New modern trains: 6 more state-of-the-art Chiltern Explorer trains will enter service as part of the December 2026 timetable, completing a fleet of 13. The new trains will increase capacity and provide improved accessibility, air conditioning and enhanced wifi for passengers between London and the West Midlands.
  • Better trains: a £12 million refurbishment of Chiltern’s existing Class 168 fleet will continue, with upgraded wifi, power and USB charging at every seat and refreshed interiors by 2028.
  • Cleaner, better stations: investment will improve stations across the network, including refurbished toilets, painting, deep cleaning and graffiti removal. At Haddenham and Thame Parkway, 200 previously closed car park spaces will be reopened, helping make it easier for passengers to access the station.
  • Better information and easier journeys: new signage at 5 of Chiltern’s busiest stations will help the almost 20 million passengers a year who use the network get to their destinations, alongside upgraded customer information screens, help points and accessible ramps. These improvements will make the railway easier to use and help customers stay informed when travelling.
  • East West Rail: public ownership also provides a fresh opportunity to deliver East West Rail and its benefits for passengers.

Tony Baxter, interim managing director of Chiltern Railways, said:

Sunday is a significant milestone for Chiltern Railways and we look forward to working together with the wider rail industry to deliver a better railway for everyone in Great Britain.

Over the next 12 months, our customers in London, Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire, Warwickshire and the West Midlands will benefit from more new trains, more services, thousands of additional seats, improvements to stations and on-board facilities and the ability to use their ticket on other operators when faced with disruption – customer improvements made possible thanks to years of planning, dedication and hard work by Chiltern colleagues.

Public ownership will further strengthen that progress through closer collaboration across the industry, helping us share best practice, drive innovation and focus on what matters most to customers, businesses and communities across our network.

The next operator’s services to transfer into public ownership will be Great Western Railway on 13 December 2026, ahead of completion of the full public ownership programme by the end of 2027.

items.title: Directors warned to verify identities with Companies House following first Insolvency Service prosecutions
items.summary: First court action for identity verification offences brought by the Insolvency Service Three directors fined after failing to comply with requirements Convictions serve as a warning to directors: verify your identity or risk prosecution Di
items.bodyHtml:
• First court action for identity verification offences brought by the Insolvency Service
  • Three directors fined after failing to comply with requirements
  • Convictions serve as a warning to directors: verify your identity or risk prosecution

Directors are being warned to verify their identities with Companies House or risk prosecution after the Insolvency Service secured its first convictions for these offences.

Jill White and Marc Dillon, directors of White (Reading Properties) Limited, and Modinat Banjo, director of J Isogony Apparel Limited, were fined at City of London Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday 16 September.

Identity verification is a central part of the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023, which strengthened Companies House powers to improve the accuracy of the company register and tackle the misuse of UK companies for criminal purposes.

Newly appointed directors have been required to verify their identity with Companies House before acting as a director from 18 November 2025.

Existing directors are required to verify during the 12-month transition period, when filing the company’s next confirmation statement, helping to ensure that those who own and control businesses can be identified and held accountable.

Daniel Hart, Senior Criminal Lawyer at the Insolvency Service, said:

Identity verification is a legal requirement for company directors and forms a key part of efforts to improve the accuracy of the Companies House register and tackle economic crime.

These prosecutions demonstrate that directors have responsibilities not only for their own compliance but also for ensuring unverified individuals do not continue acting as directors on behalf of a company.

In both cases, multiple opportunities were provided for the directors to comply with the requirements before enforcement action was taken.

There is no option to opt out. Directors who continue to act without verifying their identity risk investigation and prosecution.

Martin Swain, Director of Intelligence and Law Enforcement Engagement at Companies House, said:

These first prosecutions by the Insolvency Service for failing to comply with identity verification requirements mark an important milestone in strengthening the integrity of the UK’s company register.

Identity verification is a cornerstone of the reforms being introduced under the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act, helping to ensure that those setting up, running and controlling companies are who they claim to be.

These cases send a clear message that identity verification is not optional. The vast majority of directors and people with significant control will comply with the new requirements, but where individuals fail to meet their legal obligations, Companies House will take appropriate enforcement action.

Our goal is to create a register that is more reliable, more transparent and better equipped to support economic growth while deterring those who seek to misuse UK companies for criminal purposes.

White, 62, of Speen, Buckinghamshire, acted as a company director despite not verifying her identity. She participated in board-level decision making and signed company accounts while remaining unverified.

Indeed, White only completed identity verification in early September 2026, around nine months after the deadline and shortly before appearing in court.

Dillon, 62, of Atlanta Close, Benson, Oxfordshire, had verified his own identity. However, he was prosecuted after failing to take reasonable steps to prevent White from continuing to act as a director while unverified, despite being aware of the legal requirement.

As a director of White (Reading Properties) Limited, he had a legal responsibility to ensure the company did not allow an unverified individual to continue acting as a director.

Both were also convicted after their company failed to file a confirmation statement on time.

White was fined £166, ordered to pay costs of £85 and a victim surcharge of £66.

Dillon was fined £307, with costs of £85 and a victim surcharge of £123.

Banjo, 50, of Thornham Street, London, continued acting as a director despite also failing to complete the mandatory identity verification process. She signed and delivered company accounts on behalf of J Isogony Apparel Limited while remaining unverified.

Banjo completed identity verification only on or around 28 May 2026.

She was similarly convicted after failing to file a confirmation statement within the statutory period.

Banjo was fined £80, ordered to pay costs of £85 and a victim surcharge of £32.

Company directors who have not yet verified their identity should do so as soon as possible.

Identity verification can be completed online through Companies House free of charge or via an Authorised Corporate Service Provider.

items.title: Illegal waste site operator in Sheffield sentenced
items.summary: Defendant operated a regulated waste facility without an environmental permit. Offender received a 39-week suspended prison sentence, 180 hours of unpaid work, victim surcharge of £187 and £2,000 contribution towards prosecution costs. Two
items.bodyHtml:
• Defendant operated a regulated waste facility without an environmental permit.
  • Offender received a 39-week suspended prison sentence, 180 hours of unpaid work, victim surcharge of £187 and £2,000 contribution towards prosecution costs.
  • Two co-defendants related to the case were sentenced on 15 April 2026.
  • The site has now been cleared following Environment Agency action.

Following an investigation by the Environment Agency, Mohammed Tager, 38, of Verdon Street, Sheffield was sentenced at Sheffield Magistrates’ Court on 16 September.  He had previously pleaded guilty to operating a regulated facility without an environmental permit.

The Court sentenced Mr Tager to 39 weeks in custody suspended for 18 months, also requiring him to undertake 180 hours of unpaid work during that time. He must also pay a victim surcharge of £187, and a £2,000 contribution towards prosecution costs.

Following two successful prosecutions of Tager’s co-defendants earlier this year, the illegal waste site at the Former Stanley Works in Rutland Road, Sheffield has now been fully cleared.

More waste found at the illegal Sheffield site. Credit: Environment Agency

Ben Hocking, Area Environment Manager for the Environment Agency in Yorkshire, said:

We are glad to see Tager’s offending has been brought to justice. The case showed he had a total disregard for the law, the environment, and the local community.

He repeatedly ignored warnings and notices issued by our officers, who have worked incredibly hard to take action against him along with his co-defendants who were sentenced in April.

Following the sentencing of the co-defendants, we were pleased to see that the site has now been fully cleared.

This result shows that we’re cracking down on those flouting the regulations, and we will not hesitate to take action against those who breach the law.

Environment Agency regulatory action

The Environment Agency first visited the site on 7 July 2022 and found a large amount of mixed waste to be present. Further visits over the following months found more waste to have accumulated, including fridges and other electrical items and inert waste such as soil and stones, as well as evidence of burning.

The Environment Agency told the occupier he could not store waste without a permit, and on 10th October 2022, he was given six weeks to clear it.

In January 2023, officers inspected the site and found none of the waste had been cleared, and in fact new waste had accumulated. The Agency subsequently served a formal notice requiring the site to be cleared by 5 June 2023. The notice was not complied with.

The Environment Agency made more requests for waste to stop being brought on to the site and for it to be cleared.

In late 2024 and early 2025, complaints were received about the burning of waste, and the operator was advised by Sheffield City Council to cease burning, which was impacting on local residents.

The Environment Agency is stepping up its action on waste crime as part of its new 10 Point Plan - building on existing work and partnerships, the focused, sustained programme of action strengthens prevention, improves detection and delivers more consistent enforcement.

Anyone who suspects illegal waste activity is asked to report it to the Environment Agency’s 24-hour hotline - 0800 807060 - or anonymously contact Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

In August, Prime Minister Andy Burnham set out government plans to tackle waste crime

Background information

Two co-defendants related to the case were sentenced on 15 April 2026. The landowner, Concept Investments Limited, was fined £8,000, ordered to pay a victim surcharge of £2,000 and costs of £5,442. Austin Fitzgerald, a director of the company, was sentenced to a 12-month community order with 140 hours of unpaid work and was ordered to pay costs of £5,442 and a victim surcharge of £114.

The charges:

Between 6 July 2022 and 7 February 2024 at land known as the Former Stanley Works, Rutland Road, Sheffield, Mohammed Tager operated a regulated facility, namely a waste operation, other than under and to the extent authorised by an environmental permit.  Contrary to regulations 12(1), 38(1)(a) and 39(1) of the Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016.

Between 6 January 2025 and 23 April 2025 at land known as the Former Stanley Works, Rutland Road, Sheffield, Mohammed Tager operated a regulated facility, namely a waste operation, other than under and to the extent authorised by an environmental permit.  Contrary to regulations 12(1), 38(1)(a) and 39(1) of the Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016.

items.title: New Army accommodation completed at Upavon
items.summary: New bedspaces have been delivered for soldiers and officers at Trenchard Lines, Upavon, providing modern, sustainable living accommodation for Army personnel. At the military site in Wiltshire, 200 single en suite bedspaces are being provid
items.bodyHtml:
New bedspaces have been delivered for soldiers and officers at Trenchard Lines, Upavon, providing modern, sustainable living accommodation for Army personnel.

At the military site in Wiltshire, 200 single en suite bedspaces are being provided for junior ranks, senior ranks and officers, across separate Single Living Accommodation (SLA) blocks. An additional 21 officer bedspaces are being delivered through refurbishment of Lord House, a heritage building adjacent to the Officers’ Mess on site.

The first two completed SLA blocks have now been handed over, providing 82 bedspaces for junior ranks. The overall project is being funded under the Army’s SLA Programme and delivered by the Defence Infrastructure Organisation (DIO), contracting to Reds10 and Arcadis. 

Soldiers walking towards one of the new buildings with the other in the background. Reds10 / Richard P Walton.

At the formal opening of the completed blocks, Brigadier Grant Kerr, the Army’s Head of Infrastructure Plans, said:

The Army is making significant investment in modern accommodation that improves the lives of our people, enhances the efficiency of the estate and underpins operational readiness.

In addition to private en suite rooms, the modular SLA provides utilities, drying rooms, kitchens and furnished communal space. The building design includes sustainable features such as solar panels and energy management systems, to support day-to-day efficiency and future energy resilience.

One of the new communal areas and bedroom corridors in one of the new buildings. Reds10 / Richard P Walton.

Warren Webster, DIO MPP Army Programme Director, said:

The completion of the first new accommodation blocks at Upavon is another significant milestone in our work to provide quality, sustainable infrastructure for the Army. This new accommodation delivers environmental benefits, value for money and demonstrates our successful partnership with industry.

Phil Cook, Managing Director of Defence at Reds10, said:

Working closely with DIO and the Army, we’ve combined the benefits of industrialised construction with high-quality design to create sustainable, future-ready living spaces that put the comfort and wellbeing of Army personnel at their heart. We’re proud to be playing our part in modernising the Defence estate and delivering better accommodation for those who serve.

A further two SLA blocks are under construction at Trenchard Lines to provide 69 bedspaces for senior ranks and 49 bedspaces for officers.

Construction of all new and refurbished infrastructure at Upavon is scheduled to complete next year.

items.title: Government unveils plans to unlock over 15,000 new homes
items.summary: Plans to unlock up to 15,780 new homes in Norfolk will be published today in a first test of a new government approach to winning public consent for housebuilding. The plans, drafted by Natural England under the Nature Restoration Fund, are
items.bodyHtml:
Plans to unlock up to 15,780 new homes in Norfolk will be published today in a first test of a new government approach to winning public consent for housebuilding.  

The plans, drafted by Natural England under the Nature Restoration Fund, are part of a win-win approach to housebuilding and nature restoration, delivering the healthier wetlands and waterways people want to see in their communities alongside new housing developments.  

Rather than paying for piecemeal and costly nature mitigations as required under previous regimes, the scheme in Norfolk will see developers fund large scale improvements to rivers and wetlands across the county, which are home to species such as otters, water voles and wetland birds, and visited by millions of people each year.   

The first local blueprint, known as an Environmental Delivery Plan (EDP), will be published for consultation today by Natural England and is designed to tackle pollution in rivers and waterways across Norfolk. Pollution has been a major barrier to building new homes in parts of the county, with developers having to commission costly surveys and mitigation measures which have not done enough to restore the natural environment at scale. 

This instead gives developers a cost-effective way to deliver more effective nature restoration through a simple levy payment. This money paid by developers will then be administered by Natural England and used to deliver conservation measures at scale, improving water quality and wetlands in Norfolk, including in the iconic Norfolk Broads. 

The plan will also create new opportunities for Norfolk farmers, landowners, and private organisations to work with Natural England to deliver conservation measures to support nature recovery. 

The area earmarked for new homes and nature restoration includes the River Wensum, Bure Broads and Marshes, and Yare Broads and Marshes catchments, covering a substantial part of central and eastern Norfolk. 

Environment Secretary Angela Eagle said:  

People know there’s a housing crisis and that we must build more homes to tackle it. But people also want to live in communities they can be proud of, with thriving green spaces everyone can enjoy. 

This government rejects the false trade-off between delivering infrastructure and restoring our environment. 

Our plans are a win-win for development and nature, unlocking thousands of new homes and raising millions to improve our natural environment.

Natural England Chief Executive Marian Spain said:  

The EDP represents a new way to protect nature while also supporting growth. Instead of tackling pollution piecemeal, site by site, we can now deliver conservation measures that make a real difference for rivers, wetlands and wildlife across Norfolk.  

This will help restore the natural systems that underpin our security and protect our wellbeing, giving developers certainty that the money they need to spend is making a positive contribution to local communities.

Housing and Planning Minister Matthew Pennycook said: 

The Nature Restoration Fund established by our landmark Planning and Infrastructure Act will move us beyond the sub-optimal status quo and unlock a win-win for development and nature.

Today’s publication of the first draft Environmental Delivery Plan demonstrates in practice how the Fund will unlock and accelerate development while going beyond neutrality to drive nature recovery.

The consultation is open for 28 working days, and Natural England is inviting responses to help shape the final EDP before it is submitted to the Secretary of State.   

Natural England is also developing EDPs for other areas of the country where housebuilding is impacted by nutrient pollution in rivers. Further detail on these will be published shortly.  

Additional information:

  • The Environmental Delivery Plan, published for consultation today, sets out the conservation measures Natural England will deliver to ensure an overall improvement to nature, as required by law, and the contribution developers will need to make to use the EDP.   • The measures include restoring rivers, creating wetlands and managing fens and reedbeds. These measures will improve and reconnect habitats across the Broads and Wensum, benefiting Norfolk’s most iconic species, including otters, white-clawed crayfish, bitterns, marsh harriers and fen orchids.  

  • The EDP has been developed in conjunction with local authorities and other local partners to reflect the environmental priorities in Norfolk. 

  • The EDP provides a strategic delivery plan to support up to 15,780 homes across Norfolk and the charges developers will pay to take part. It provides certainty and a streamlined process; with developers paying a simple, flat rate to fund environmental improvements in Norfolk. The money is ringfenced and will be spent on conservation measures in Norfolk as well as long term monitoring and maintenance. 

  • The consultation is open for 28 working days, and Natural England is inviting responses to help shape the final EDP before it comes into force. The requirement to consult on each Environmental Delivery Plan will ensure that communities, developers and environmental groups are able to properly scrutinise Environmental Delivery Plans before they are made.   

  • Natural England has notified the Secretary of State that they are developing Environmental Delivery Plans for other areas of the country affected by nutrient pollution. Further detail on the timelines for future Environmental Delivery Plans will be published shortly. 

  • Natural England, MHCLG and Defra have recently published guidance on using the Nature Restoration Levy process and we will be publishing further guidance in due course on other elements of the new system.

items.title: ‘People’s Power’ projects to give more control over local energy
items.summary: Great British Energy rolls out first wave of biggest public community energy investment in UK history, backing local places to cut bills and take climate action Local authorities and community energy groups can now access funding to build t
items.bodyHtml:
• Great British Energy rolls out first wave of biggest public community energy investment in UK history, backing local places to cut bills and take climate action
  • Local authorities and community energy groups can now access funding to build their own clean power projects
  • Communities to be offered an ownership stake in renewable energy projects, ensuring proceeds of clean power flow back into local areas

Communities across the country will be able to build and control their own clean energy supply that will help to cut bills, grow local wealth and tackle the climate crisis – with the rollout of People’s Power projects across the UK.

Local authorities and community energy groups across the UK will now be able to progress plans for their own clean power projects - from solar panels on local buildings to village-owned wind farms and hydro schemes in nearby rivers. This will help to put money back in the pockets of communities and allow them to join in UK-wide climate action, following the record temperatures reached this summer due to climate change.

Great British Energy is today (Thursday 17 September) launching £30 million funding to kick start a community power revolution – the first downpayment on up to £1 billion, announced earlier this year, with the aim to support over 1,000 local and community-led clean energy projects across the UK. These will be owned by community energy groups or local authorities, meaning local areas can reap the full benefits – from reduced bills for local services to ensuring profits from the clean power generated flow back into towns and villages, rather than just to energy companies.

After the heatwaves and extreme weather events seen this year, this funding will give communities a route to helping tackle climate change - empowering them to move away from fossil fuels with their own clean energy supply that will help cut emissions and protect their local area.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:

I know many people are worried about climate change and feel like they’ve got no control over where their energy comes from, or how they can actually make a difference.

Today we’re changing that by giving people power. Whether it’s solar panels on a local library or a community-owned wind farm, we’re letting people decide what clean energy projects they want and making sure they feel the benefits of the clean energy transition in their pockets too.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said:

All of us felt deep concern for our climate during the record-breaking temperatures we experienced this summer.

Ahead of New York Climate week, we are putting power in the hands of people and places, so more communities can take action.

Everyone deserves a stake in our energy future and through these local power projects, communities can reap the full benefits of clean energy – reducing emissions, cutting bills and reinvesting profits to benefit local areas, instead of big energy companies.

CEO of Great British Energy Dan McGrail said:

Great British Energy is continuing to put communities at the heart of the clean energy transition with the GBE Community Fund and Partnerships Grant. Our vision is that every community should have the chance to build and own its own renewable energy. These grants will give community organisations and local authorities the practical support they need to get clean energy projects off the ground - lowering bills, supporting jobs and putting the benefits from energy into local hands.

Alongside funding specific local power projects, the government will also set out further details this Autumn on plans for community energy groups to be offered an ownership stake in renewable energy projects.

This aims to create partnerships between communities and developers that will see proceeds of clean power flow back into local areas. It will bring Britain in line with countries like Germany and Denmark, where this type of ownership set up is already widely used – allowing communities to benefit directly from local clean power.

It comes as a host of Great British Energy schemes come online, helping local services save on energy bills in towns and cities across England. Over 150 renewable projects have now switched-on for public buildings in England’s Mayoral Combined Authorities, with more to follow – which together could see up to £50 million in total energy bill savings reinvested in local services.

Notes to editors

Local ownership is already breathing new life into neighbourhoods across the country, reviving pubs, libraries and leisure centres. But for too long, community-run energy projects have been held back by a lack of funding, advice and government support.

Great British Energy is changing this as applications have opened today for new grants to support community energy projects in England, Wales and Northern Ireland - while £1.8 million has been allocated to the Scottish Government for its existing community energy support programme. It forms the first wave of up to £1 billion in support to put clean energy back in the hand of communities.

This is on top of up to £16 million in Great British Energy support already provided to all Mayoral Combined Authorities in England to help local services save on bills with 157 new rooftop solar projects now installed - from fire stations to leisure centres.

The Great British Energy support launched today includes:

  • The £20 million Community Fund – offers grant funding to help community organisations across England, Wales and Northern Ireland to test, develop and build community-owned clean energy assets. Projects supported by this fund must demonstrate that the community will hold a defined legal and financial interest in the project, and that a defined share of project benefits will be retained for, or delivered to, the local community.
  • The £5 million Partnerships Grant – a new scheme offering grant funding to help Local Authorities in England and community energy partners accelerate joint clean energy projects that will provide lasting local benefits.
  • £1.8 million in Great British Energy funding for the Scottish Government to back community energy projects across Scotland, building on more than £10 million provided earlier this year. This will support Scotland’s existing community energy support schemes, under the Scottish Government’s CARES programme.
  • Advice services – Great British Energy is also backing organisations that offer crucial advice to local groups on the development of community energy initiatives with up to £2.9 million support for advice services across England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Great British Energy is also seeking information from investors to help size and scope its future products.

CEO of Community Energy England Dr Matt Vickers said:

Community Energy England welcomes the GBE Community Fund as the first step in the £1bn investment in community and local energy in the Local Power Plan. This will enable community enterprises across the country to deliver projects which will reduce bills, create a more resilient and cleaner energy system and most importantly keep the benefits of energy in the communities where it’s generated.  

We’ve long advocated for the new Partnership Fund so councils and community enterprises can work together to transform places.

items.summary: The Prime Minister met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney this evening, before the two leaders watched their football club Everton play. The leaders began by underscoring the close cooperation between the UK and Canada and emphasised the i
items.bodyHtml:
The Prime Minister met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney this evening, before the two leaders watched their football club Everton play.

The leaders began by underscoring the close cooperation between the UK and Canada and emphasised the importance of building similar close ties with European partners, particularly on trade and defence.

The Prime Minister welcomed Canada becoming the first observer nation in the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) this summer, as the leaders discussed strengthening defence cooperation and the complementary work of the Multilateral Defence Mechanism and the Defence Security Resilience Bank.

The leaders also discussed the opportunities and challenges presented by artificial intelligence, agreeing on the importance of governments and the technology sector working together to address shared concerns and protect online safety.

The leaders looked forward to speaking again soon.

items.title: PM meeting with NATO Secretary General, Mark Rutte: 16 September 2026
items.summary: The Prime Minister hosted the NATO Secretary General, Mark Rutte, at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus this afternoon. The Prime Minister began by thanking the Secretary General for his visit to Oxford and the opportunity to highlig
items.bodyHtml:
The Prime Minister hosted the NATO Secretary General, Mark Rutte, at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus this afternoon.

The Prime Minister began by thanking the Secretary General for his visit to Oxford and the opportunity to highlight the fantastic defence businesses in the region.

The two leaders agreed that the UK was a leader in defence technology and they discussed how the UK could further support innovation within NATO to ensure the Alliance had the forces of the future across all domains.

The new national space strategy, released last week, would further enhance the UK’s innovation and resilience in the space domain too, the Prime Minister added.

Turning to Ukraine, the Prime Minister reflected on his visit to Kyiv last month and said he was focused on supporting diplomatic efforts to secure further air defence for the country.

The Secretary General thanked the Prime Minister for the UK’s £100m PURL funding contribution for further defensive equipment announced last week.  

On the Middle East, both underlined the importance of ensuring long term stability and security in the region.

The leaders looked forward to speaking again soon.

items.bodyHtml:
Defence Secretary Rt Hon Wes Streeting MP said:

No family should have to go through the loss that Jaysley-Louise’s family are having to deal with every single day. My thoughts are with her family and loved ones. I commend the bravery and determination they have shown in pursuing the change needed in our Armed Forces.

Every person who serves in our Armed Forces is owed a duty of care, and all have a responsibility to uphold standards of behaviour befitting the uniform they wear.

The Army has accepted all of the findings identified by the Service Inquiry and responded to the recommendations to improve Service life across its culture, policies, and practices.

While significant reforms have been introduced since Jaysley-Louise’s tragic death, including commissioning the first-ever Armed Forces sexualised behaviour and sexual harassment survey, appointing the first Armed Forces Commissioner, and strengthening the Victim Witness Care Unit and Defence Serious Crime Command, there is more to do.

I am deeply committed to improving how complaints and crimes are reported and investigated. Service personnel must have confidence that unacceptable and criminal behaviour will be tackled, that concerns will be acted upon, and that they will be supported when they come forward. Jaysley-Louise’s family have my commitment that I will continue to drive the changes needed to ensure every voice is heard.

I encourage anyone who has experienced a sexual offence to seek support and report it. Information on reporting options, specialist support services and help available within and outside Defence can be found on the Defence support: sexual offences guidance on GOV.UK.

Brigadier Melissa Emmett, Head of Army Personnel Services Group (APSG), speaking on behalf of the Chief of the General Staff and the Army, said:  

To Jaysley-Louise’s family, we remain deeply sorry for the circumstances surrounding her death, and reiterate my and the Army’s deepest condolences to you, her family, and to her friends.

The conclusion of this independent court martial brings the legal process in this case to an end., We recognise the impact that this process has had on all those involved and that there is no outcome that will lessen the profound loss Jaysley-Louise’s family continues to live with every day.  

In the years since Jaysley-Louise’s untimely death, the Army has acted on the findings of the service inquiry, the inquest, and subsequent investigations as we seek to drive improvements to our culture. We are raising expectations of behaviour, strengthening leadership at every level, and improving the way concerns are reported and addressed. Our focus is on creating an environment where people feel confident and safe to speak up, where reports of unacceptable or criminal behaviour are taken seriously, and where prompt and appropriate action follows.

Those personnel who have been subject to these proceedings will continue to receive all appropriate support and must be enabled to return to duties as serving members of the Army.

We are determined to build a culture founded on respect, trust and accountability, and to continue our work to stamp out abuse and unacceptable behaviour affecting our people. We encourage anyone who believes they have been a victim of a crime to report it to the police.

items.title: Salmon numbers in England hit lowest level on record
items.summary: New research from the Environment Agency (EA), Cefas and Natural Resources Wales confirms salmon stocks in England are at their lowest level since records began. The Atlantic Salmon Stock Assessment for 2025 shows 95% of principal salmon ri
items.bodyHtml:
New research from the Environment Agency (EA), Cefas and Natural Resources Wales confirms salmon stocks in England are at their lowest level since records began. 

The Atlantic Salmon Stock Assessment for 2025 shows 95% of principal salmon rivers are now below the level needed to sustain their populations. This is up from 88% in last year’s assessment, and the highest level recorded to date. In the past, 15 to 20 young salmon out of every 100 that migrated to sea would return as adults, now only one or two do.

This problem is not unique to England and is observable across the North Atlantic. Much of the cause lies at sea and beyond the control of any single country. However, the EA is taking action to address the decline by removing barriers that block salmon from reaching their spawning grounds, cracking down on pollution and illegal water abstraction, restoring rivers and wetlands and pushing for international action to tackle threats at sea. 

In rivers, analysis has shown that the decline in stocks is being driven by water quantity, water quality and damaged habitat. As part of our reporting to the North Atlantic Salmon Conservation Organisation (NASCO), we have set out new commitments to tackle all three issues by 2032.

Under these new commitments, the EA will restore 2,282 hectares of peatland and improve water flow below reservoirs, so rivers have enough water, even during dry spells. It will also closely monitor water companies and other users to ensure they are not taking more water than rivers can sustain. 

Alongside this, the EA will continue to increase its inspections of farms and wastewater treatment works more often, and fund over 800 projects to cut pollution from wastewater. It will also clear or improve 105 barriers blocking salmon from their spawning grounds, restore habitat at 252 sites, and plant trees along 648 hectares of riverbank to keep water cool and clean.

Environment Agency Chief Executive Philip Duffy said: 

These figures are stark. Where 15 to 20 salmon once returned from every 100 that went to sea, now it’s as few as one or two.

Recovery requires collective action. On the Trent and the Ouse, targeted initiatives have already brought salmon back and we now need to go further to see this pattern replicated across the country.

This year the EA and its partners have committed to restore over 2,000 hectares of peatland, improve fish passage at over 100 migration barriers, and deliver more than 250 habitat restoration projects on principal salmon rivers by 2032.

Salmon are returning to the River Trent and River Ouse following efforts led by the EA to improve water quality and remove barriers to migration, demonstrating that recovery is possible where key pressures are tackled.

The EA is also working with partners across the country to help salmon recover. In Yorkshire, the Great Yorkshire Rivers Partnership is reconnecting rivers and reopening fish passage, giving migratory fish access to habitat they haven’t reached for generations. The return of salmon to parts of the River Don in recent years shows what is possible when rivers are restored and migration routes are reconnected.

Later this year, the EA will publish the next round of River Basin Management Plans which will show that to protect fish, it will need to go faster in removing unnecessary weirs and barriers that impede fish migration.

items.title: Chancellor announces Bank of England appointments
items.summary: David Craig and Paul Nowak are appointed to four-year terms until 31 August 2030. Hanneke Smits will begin her four-year term on 1 January 2027, until 31 December 2030. David Craig and Paul Nowak take up the positions vacated by Sir Ron Kal
items.bodyHtml:
David Craig and Paul Nowak are appointed to four-year terms until 31 August 2030. Hanneke Smits will begin her four-year term on 1 January 2027, until 31 December 2030.  

David Craig and Paul Nowak take up the positions vacated by Sir Ron Kalifa and Baroness Frances O’Grady.  David Craig and Paul Nowak will attend their first Court meetings on 17 September and 22 October respectively. Hanneke Smits will take up the position currently held by Sabine Chalmers, who has informed the Court of her intention to resign her role at the end of October 2026, and Hanneke Smits will attend her first Court meeting on 11 February 2027. 

These new appointments come alongside the reappointment of Lord Jitesh Gadhia and Tom Shropshire as non-executive directors for a second four-year team. Lord Jitesh Gadhia will begin his four-year term on the 24 October 2026, and Tom Shropshire will begin his four-year term on the 1 November 2026.

Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, said:  

These appointments strengthen the Court at a critical moment for the UK economy, providing deep and varied experience to support the Bank in delivering its core missions of monetary and financial stability.

David Roberts, Chair of Court, said: 

The Governor and I wish to thank Sabine Chalmers for her dedication to the Bank of England over the past four years and the insights she has brought to the Court throughout that time, including her support for the Bank’s culture and people development agenda. 

On behalf of Court, I am delighted to welcome David, Paul and Hanneke, who bring considerable insight and experience that will aid the Court in executing on our responsibilities. I look forward to continuing working with Jitesh and Tom following their reappointment, as we continue to drive forward the changes needed to ensure the Bank is well placed to deliver in the coming years.

About Paul Nowak  

Paul Nowak is General Secretary of the Trades Union Congress. The TUC represents 47 unions and 5.3 million workers in the UK. Paul has represented the TUC internationally at the International Labour Organisation, OECD and G20, and holds non-executive experience at Unity Trust Bank.

About David Craig  

David Craig is a senior financial markets and data technology executive with over 30 years’ leadership experience. He founded and led Refinitiv as CEO, building it into a global leader in financial data, technology and trading platforms before instigating its acquisition by London Stock Exchange Group, where he subsequently led the Data and Analytics Division. Amongst other financial industry technology and data roles, he co-chairs the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures.

About Hanneke Smits  

Hanneke Smits is a senior investment management executive with 34 years’ experience, including as former Global Head of BNY Investment Management and a member of BNY’s Executive Committee. Whilst at BNY Hanneke also served on a few subsidiary asset management boards (Alcentra, Insight, Newton and Walter Scott). She has previously served on the Court and brings extensive non-executive experience across the Wellcome Trust, the Van Leer Foundation and the Education Endowment Foundation. 

About Lord Jitesh Gadhia  

Lord Gadhia has over 25 years’ investment banking and financial services experience, having held senior positions at Blackstone, Barclays Capital, ABN AMRO and Baring Brothers. He currently serves on the boards of Rolls-Royce Holdings plc and Taylor Wimpey plc, and previously served on the boards of UK Financial Investments Limited and UK Government Investments Limited from 2014 to 2022. He has been a member of the House of Lords since 2016. He is also Chair of The British Asian Trust, a charitable foundation established by His Majesty King Charles III.

About Tom Shropshire  

Tom Shropshire is Senior Vice President and General Counsel of Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc. Prior to this, he was General Counsel and Company Secretary of Diageo plc. Before joining Diageo, he was a partner at Linklaters LLP, where he was Global Head of US Practice and co-head of the Risk and Resilience Practice. He is a trustee of the New York University School of Law and a former trustee and chair of Comic Relief.

About the Court of the Bank of England   

The Court of the Bank of England acts as the Bank’s board. It is responsible for overseeing the Bank’s strategy, governance, budget and risk framework, and for ensuring the effective discharge of the Bank’s statutory functions. 

The Court consists of the Chair and eight other Non-Executive Directors, the Governor and four Deputy Governors. Non-Executive Directors bring independent judgement and a breadth of experience to the Court’s deliberations.

About the appointment process  

The appointment followed a fair and open competition in line with the Governance Code on Public Appointments. 

Appointments and reappointments to the Court of the Bank of England are not automatic. Each case is considered on its own merits. 

David Craig, Paul Nowak, Hanneke Smits, Lord Jitesh Gadhia and Tom Shropshire have confirmed that they have not engaged in any significant party political activity in the last five years.

items.title: UK calls for calm following Kosovo Specialist Chambers judgment
items.summary: Minister for Europe, Lord Wood of Anfield said: “The UK respects the independence of the Court and its judicial process and remains committed to justice, accountability and reconciliation across the region. “The UK remains a close friend an
items.bodyHtml:
Minister for Europe, Lord Wood of Anfield said:

“The UK respects the independence of the Court and its judicial process and remains committed to justice, accountability and reconciliation across the region.

“The UK remains a close friend and partner of Kosovo, firmly supporting its sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity, as well as peace across the Western Balkans. We are proud of the role we played alongside NATO Allies in helping prevent a humanitarian catastrophe in 1999 and in supporting Kosovo’s independence in 2008.

”Today’s judgment by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers is a significant moment but it is not a judgment on Kosovo’s statehood, sovereignty or right to determine its own future. The thoughts of the UK Government are with the victims and their families.

“The Court’s findings concern individuals and should not be used to inflame tensions between communities or across the region.  At this important moment, political leaders and public figures have a responsibility to promote calm, ensure any reactions remain peaceful, and put people’s safety first.

“The UK will continue to work with partners across the region and beyond to support peace, justice, and a secure and prosperous future for all communities.”

items.title: Public encouraged to submit their memories of Queen Elizabeth II as 4th anniversary of late monarch’s passing is marked
items.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people have visited the Queen Elizabeth Digital Memorial since its launch on 21 April this year, as part of the national memorial, with many people, including famous faces, submitting their personal memories. Led by
items.bodyHtml:
Hundreds of thousands of people have visited the Queen Elizabeth Digital Memorial since its launch on 21 April this year, as part of the national memorial, with many people, including famous faces, submitting their personal memories. 

Led by the Cabinet Office, the digital memorial brings together rich archive material, photography and video to map key events from Queen Elizabeth’s life and reign, and invites the public from around the world to contribute their own memories to create a lasting public record.

Today, working alongside major organisations such as Barnardos, the Scottish Women’s Institute, the National Gallery, the London Ambulance Service and others, the digital memorial will release rarely seen archival photographs and memories of the late Queen’s life to mark the fourth anniversary.

The website is underpinned by a searchable, complete record of Queen Elizabeth’s public engagements and duties across the entirety of her reign from 1952 to 2022. Anyone can visit the site, search for a particular date to see what the Queen was doing, or search a location to see if the Queen visited it. The website has also brought together collections and archives across the UK including the Royal Collection and the BBC, releasing a collection of rarely seen films ranging from her wedding in 1947 through to the Diamond Jubilee Pageant in 2012. 

New material released today includes: 

  • A new memory from Sir Stephen Fry touching on the collective sense of loss he felt with those in the audience at a test match in Oval when the announcement of the late Queen’s passing was announced.
  • Images and objects from the National Gallery relating to Queen Elizabeth’s visit in 1991 to open the Sainsbury wing.
  • Images of young children celebrating with a birthday cake sent by Princess Elizabeth to the Barnardo’s Girls Village Home in Barkingside in 1936;
  • An audio recording of a member’s memory from the Scottish Women’s Institutes on Royal Deeside, following a two-year project funded by The National Lottery Heritage Fund as the organisation approaches its 110th anniversary in 2027.
  • Images and objects from the London Ambulance Service NHS Trust from Queen Elizabeth’s visit to their headquarters in 1975.

His Royal Highness The Prince of Wales recently shared his favourite memories of the late Queen on the platform. Other notable public figures who have provided memories include the Hon Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey, Secretary-General of the Commonwealth, Tom Daley OBE, Dame Tracey Emin, Baroness Valerie Amos, and others. 

The Queen Elizabeth Digital Memorial is now inviting the public to share a memory of Queen Elizabeth that has stayed with them. You may have performed for the Queen in a choir, met her on a walkabout in your town, celebrated one of her jubilees with your local community; whatever it is – we want to hear it. 

Don’t miss the chance to share your memories of Queen Elizabeth for her centenary year. Add yours today at www.queenelizabeth.com.

ENDS

  • Princess Elizabeth gifts cake to Barnardo’s Girls Village Home, 1936
  • Opening of the Sainsbury Wing, The National Gallery, 1991
  • Memories of a SWI member, 1953
  • Visit to the London Ambulance Service, 1975

items.summary: The operator of three illegal waste sites near Harleston has been issued a hefty £20,000 fine and a 5-year criminal behaviour order (CBO) after dumping, burying, and burning waste between October 2023 and July 2024. In addition, David Pipe,
items.bodyHtml:
The operator of three illegal waste sites near Harleston has been issued a hefty £20,000 fine and a 5-year criminal behaviour order (CBO) after dumping, burying, and burning waste between October 2023 and July 2024.

In addition, David Pipe, director of D M Pipe Ltd, RRAGO Jack Leasing Ltd and RRAGO Jack Recruitment Ltd, received a 12-month custodial sentence, suspended for 18 months.

You have had enough time. With respect to you, this [removing the waste] will be your priority. The position in this case is not regulatory misunderstanding or uncertainty. Judge condemns operator – ‘You knew what the notices required and chose not to do so’

Pipe was invited to a voluntary interview under caution. When no reply was forthcoming, Officers revisited the site and saw waste still there.  The Environment Agency then wrote to inform Pipe warning him of potential legal action.  Further visits were made culminating in a final inspection made on 23 March 2026 which showed little effort had been made to clear the site.

Lesley Robertson, enforcement team leader at the Environment Agency in Norfolk, said:

Where we find evidence of illegal activity, we will not hesitate to take enforcement action; the suspended sentence and CBO show how seriously the court views waste crime.

Councillor Tristan Gale, Suffolk County Council’s cabinet member for planning, devolution and the fire service, said:

I welcome this outcome, which sends a clear message that breaches of planning and environmental regulations will not be tolerated. I would like to thank Suffolk County Council officers and the Environment Agency for their work in bringing this case before the courts. We will continue to work with our partners to protect Suffolk’s communities, environment and law-abiding businesses.

David Mark Pipe was charged with two waste offences:

  1. Between 23 October 2023 and 16 July 2024 at Withersdale Hall, Metfield, Harleston, IP20 0JR did operate a regulated facility, namely a waste operation for the deposit, treatment and storage of waste, except under and to the extent authorised by an environmental permit contrary to regulations 12 and 38(1)(a) Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016.

  2. By 13 May 2024, failed, without reasonable excuse to comply with a notice dated 16 February 2024 and served on you on pursuant to section 59(1)(a) of the Environmental Protection Act 1990 in that you failed to remove controlled waste from land at Withersdale Hall Metfield, Harleston, IP20 0JR and failed to provide evidence of the lawful removal of controlled waste contrary to section 59(5) Environmental Protection Act 1990.

Background:

  • The Environment Agency’s ten-point plan is taking the fight against waste criminals up a gear. Specialist officers are acting earlier on larger sites, sharing more information with the public, making greater use of enforcement tools, and actively naming and shaming illegal waste sites.
  • The Environment Agency has secured almost 250 prosecutions for waste offences across England since 2023, with courts handing out fines of more than £2.2m and nearly 90 custodial or suspended prison sentences.
  • In 2024/25 alone, the Environment Agency closed 743 illegal waste sites over the country. Some 143 were high risk.
  • The Environment Agency’s economic crime unit has secured more than £1.5m in confiscation orders in recent years, along with freezing almost £21m through investigations into money laundering linked to waste crime.
